content:
"Northern Territory police had failed time and time again, and everyone seemed to know it except the people who could have done something about it.

Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23, sat behind the vegetation on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, cradling a young woman he had only met hours before at a bar. The Toyota Hilux that had carried them both through the Darwin night was now wrapped around a palm tree, its hood crumpled like discarded paper. The woman drifted in and out of consciousness, her back injured, her breathing shallow. Dale held her tightly, as if somehow that could undo what had happened.

He had been drinking. The officers who stumbled upon the scene — originally heading to investigate a noise complaint — noted his blood alcohol reading at 0.149, nearly three times the legal limit. They had not been looking for him. They had simply found him, the way fate sometimes arranges these terrible meetings.

What happened next would become the subject of a coroner's inquest, one that would expose years of institutional negligence and bureaucratic inaction. NT Coroner Greg Cavanagh would later find that Northern Territory police had ignored a 2013 internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged police vehicles — a recommendation that had come following a previous death in custody.

In the three years between that earlier death and Dale's, at least sixteen people had attempted suicide in the back of those same caged vehicles. Sixteen times the warning bells had rung. In six of those cases, the individuals were not detected until they were already semi-conscious or unconscious, hanging somewhere between life and death in the darkness of a police van while officers drove on, unaware.

'It wasn't a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when,' Cavanagh concluded, his words carrying the weight of an inevitability that should never have been allowed to become inevitable.

Dale Walkinshaw was a vulnerable young man. Whatever had brought him to that bar, to that car, to that palm tree on that particular September night in Darwin, he was now in the custody of the state. And the state, as it had done so many times before, was not prepared to keep him safe.

The cameras were never installed. The report gathered dust. And the caged vehicles continued to carry their passengers through the Northern Territory night, unseen and unwatched, until it was too late."
